paras: The lynching of Bishop Emberton and Richard Speakman took place in Kentucky on or about August 1, 1882, when a mob took the two white men from a guard moving them from the Tompkinsville jail to Glasgow and killed them about thirteen miles from Glasgow. The men had been charged with assaulting Mrs. J. B. Garrett near Tompkinsville in Monroe County. The killing was carried by wire across the country, and several papers headlined it as deserved or justified.

According to a Glasgow letter printed in the Breckenridge News, Mrs. Garrett lived about a mile from Tompkinsville, and her husband was away in Tennessee on business when the assault was alleged to have occurred. Garrett's father summoned neighbors, who captured the two men around daybreak the next morning, and Mrs. Garrett identified them. After an examining trial the men were jailed at Tompkinsville in default of bail.

A second Glasgow letter reported that threats of lynching were freely spoken and that a release by friends of the prisoners was also feared, so a heavy guard watched the jail from Friday until Monday night. That night the county judge ordered the men transferred to the Barren County jail at Glasgow for safekeeping.

Early the next morning a wagon carrying the prisoners and a guard, put at fifteen men, left Tompkinsville for Glasgow. About thirteen miles from Glasgow on the Tompkinsville road, the guard was overtaken by armed men who compelled the surrender of the two prisoners. The first Glasgow letter said the men were at once taken to a tree and hanged, and the Interior Journal of Stanford also reported that they were hung. The Courier-Journal's Glasgow special, by contrast, said they were shot to death, and the Hickman Courier later combined the versions, saying they were hung to a tree and riddled with bullets.

The second Glasgow letter remarked that the wagon had not reached Glasgow, that the state would have no more expense, and that the governor had lost an opportunity to exercise the pardoning power. No report of an inquest, an arrest of the lynchers or a grand jury inquiry appears in the coverage.

The first notice came in a Courier-Journal special from Glasgow, sent out from Louisville on August 2 and printed the next day in the Wheeling Daily Intelligencer under the headline 'Deserved Their Fate'. The St. Paul Daily Globe ran the dispatch as 'Received Their Just Dues', the Savannah Morning News headed its item 'Speedy Vengeance', and the Bismarck Tribune used 'Shot Like Dogs'. Through mid-August the story circulated in one-sentence roundup items in weeklies from Minnesota and Wisconsin to Mississippi and Virginia, some saying the men were 'overtaken by avengers' and others that they were 'lynched by a mob'.

Kentucky papers gave fuller and more openly approving accounts. The Breckenridge News of Cloverport printed both Glasgow letters under the heading 'A Justifiable Lynching', describing the woman as a lady of eminent respectability and saying that the little band of six had done what a thousand would have been glad to help with. Year-end chronologies in Michigan papers recalled the case without names as two men lynched at Tompkinsville on July 30 'for maltreating a white woman'.

Accounts differ on how the men died: the wire said they were shot, the Breckenridge News and Interior Journal said hanged, and the Hickman Courier said both. The date also varies, with most reports giving August 1, the Lancaster Daily Intelligencer's version saying the transfer was on Monday, and the year-end lists giving July 30. The two Glasgow letters disagree on the alleged assault, one placing it at about two in the afternoon and the other at about one in the morning with chloroform, and on the attackers, one describing a large force and the other a band some put at six. Wire reports placed the alleged crime on Tuesday of the previous week, while the St. Paul Daily Globe's version said Sunday.

reader.title: Lynching of Bishop Emberton and Richard Speakman
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
bases: A mob took two white prisoners charged with assaulting a woman from a guard taking them to the Glasgow jail and killed them (A6, A12, A13, A29).

Both men were killed by a mob or band (six in one account, a 'large force' in another) that seized them from a lawful guard, in punishment for an alleged assault on Mrs. Garrett (A12, A13, A29). The victims are described as white, so the episode is not anti-Black violence (A13).

The Courier-Journal wire, two independent Glasgow letters in the Breckenridge News, and separate Kentucky items in the Interior Journal and Hickman Courier agree that the men were killed while being moved to Glasgow (A6, A12, A13, A29).

accounts.gist: The two men, charged with an 'unspeakable crime' against Mrs. Garrett, were shot to death thirteen miles from Glasgow while being brought there for safekeeping.

accounts.label: First Glasgow letter (Breckenridge News)
accounts.gist: A large force overtook a guard of fifteen on the Tompkinsville road, compelled the surrender of the men and hanged them at a tree; proof of guilt was called so strong that none thought them undeserving.

accounts.label: Second Glasgow letter (Breckenridge News)
accounts.gist: After a heavy guard watched the Tompkinsville jail from Friday to Monday night, the county judge ordered a transfer; friends of the woman, a band some say of only six, intercepted the wagon, which 'has not yet reached Glasgow'.

accounts.label: Kentucky items (Interior Journal, Hickman Courier)
accounts.gist: The men were overtaken by a mob en route to the Barren County jail and hanged; the Hickman Courier adds that they were riddled with bullets.

framing.detail: The Breckenridge News headed its Glasgow letters 'A Justifiable Lynching' and praised 'the little band' of six.
Wire headlines 'Deserved Their Fate' (Wheeling) and 'Received Their Just Dues' (St. Paul) endorsed the killing.
The Bismarck Tribune ran the same wire under 'Shot Like Dogs'.
Weekly roundups across the Midwest and South repeated one-sentence versions, some saying 'avengers' or 'a mob'.

conflicts.note: The Kentucky letters are fuller, but none names a witness.
The second Glasgow letter's sequence (jail guarded through Monday night, wagon left early next morning) fits August 1; the other dates come from a single wire variant and a later chronology.
The second Glasgow letter places it in the night after the men passed through Tompkinsville on Tuesday evening.
